entries.label: adjective + preposition
entries.meaning: To be likely to be affected or changed by something, or to depend on something such as approval or a rule.
entries.usage: Common in official notices, contracts, terms and conditions and the news: *subject to change*, *subject to approval*, *subject to a fee*. Here *subject* is an adjective, stressed on the first syllable, and it is followed by a noun. Do not confuse it with the passive verb *be subjected to*, which means to be forced to experience something unpleasant.
entries.pattern: be subject to + change / approval / tax / a fee
examples: Flight times **are subject to** change, depending on the weather.
Our apartment **is subject to** rent control, so the landlord can only raise the rent a little each year.
Packages from overseas **are subject to** customs fees, which can be surprisingly high.

drill.sentence: Your year-end bonus {{is subject to}} federal and state income tax, so the check will be smaller than you think.
drill.hint: will be affected by (official wording, as in tax rules)

mistake.wrong: All prices are subjected to change.
mistake.right: All prices are subject to change.
mistake.why: *Subjected to* is a passive verb meaning *forced to experience* something bad; for things that may change or depend on a rule, use the adjective *subject to*.

entries.related: *depend on* — plainer; *conditional on* — formal, only if a condition is met; *exempt from* — the opposite, not affected by a rule.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The most important beliefs and principles of a person or organization, which guide their decisions and behavior.
entries.usage: Very common in business (company websites, job interviews, mission statements) and in talk about personal identity. In corporate language it can sound like empty jargon, so people sometimes use it ironically. Typical verbs are *share*, *reflect*, *stay true to* and *live by*.
entries.pattern: share / reflect / stay true to + someone's core values
examples: Honesty and kindness are the **core values** my parents tried to teach us.
In the interview, they asked how my experience reflects the company's **core values**.
The coach benched his star player, saying respect for teammates is one of the team's **core values**.

drill.sentence: The school's three {{core values}} — respect, effort and kindness — are painted above the front door.
drill.hint: its most central principles — two words (not *guiding principles*)

entries.related: *principles* — rules you follow, often moral; *mission statement* — a company's official description of its purpose; *core beliefs* — similar, more about what you think is true.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To officially introduce penalties, such as limits on trade, money or travel, against a country, company or person to punish them or force a change in behavior.
entries.usage: Mainly in news and international politics; the subject is usually a government or an international body. The pattern is *impose sanctions on* (or *against*) a country or person, and the opposite is *lift sanctions*. *Impose* also goes with *a fine*, *a ban*, *a tax* and *restrictions*.
entries.pattern: impose sanctions on / against + country / company / person
examples: The UN **imposed sanctions** on the country after it tested a nuclear weapon.
Several governments **imposed sanctions** on the general and froze his bank accounts abroad.
Because of the **sanctions imposed** on the country, our company can't ship spare parts there anymore.

drill.sentence: After the army took power, several neighboring countries {{imposed sanctions}} on the new government and stopped all trade with it.
drill.hint: officially put penalties in place (not *placed* or *introduced*)

entries.related: *lift sanctions* — end them; *impose a ban / a fine* — the same verb with other penalties; *embargo* — a complete ban on trade with a country.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Very sick with an illness that could be dangerous or even threaten someone's life.
entries.usage: Common in news, medical contexts and careful conversation, often as *become seriously ill* or *seriously ill patients*. In everyday American speech *really sick* is more common, and *ill* sounds more formal than *sick*. *Critically ill* is stronger: the patient is in immediate danger.
entries.pattern: be / become seriously ill / seriously ill + patients / children
examples: Her father was **seriously ill** last winter, so she moved back home to take care of him.
Only the most **seriously ill** patients are admitted to the ICU.
Several people became **seriously ill** after eating contaminated oysters, health officials said.

drill.sentence: When my brother became {{seriously ill}} with pneumonia, the whole family flew in to see him.
drill.hint: dangerously sick — the more formal adverb + adjective (not *critically …* or *very sick*)

mistake.why: *Heavily ill* is a word-for-word translation of German *schwer krank*; English uses *seriously*, *very* or *critically ill*.

entries.related: *critically ill* — in immediate danger of dying; *terminally ill* — will die of the illness; *under the weather* — informal, only slightly sick.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Personal and social abilities, such as communication, teamwork and managing your time, as opposed to technical knowledge.
entries.usage: Common in job ads, HR, career advice and performance reviews; the opposite is *hard skills* (technical, measurable abilities). It is usually plural: *strong soft skills*, *improve your soft skills*. In casual talk people often say *people skills* instead.
entries.pattern: have / develop / improve + (strong) soft skills
examples: He's a brilliant coder, but his **soft skills** need work: he interrupts everyone in meetings.
Teachers say team sports help kids build **soft skills** like patience and cooperation.
Nurses with strong **soft skills** can calm a frightened patient in minutes.

drill.sentence: Our new manager isn't very technical, but her {{soft skills}} are excellent: she listens, stays calm and gives clear feedback.
drill.hint: personal and social abilities (not *people …* or *interpersonal …*)

entries.related: *hard skills* — technical abilities you can measure; *people skills* — informal, the ability to deal with people; *interpersonal skills* — more formal, used in job ads.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To create a detailed plan for reaching a goal, usually over a longer period of time.
entries.usage: Common in business, sports, politics and personal planning. *Develop* suggests careful work over time; *come up with a strategy* is more casual, and *devise a strategy* is more formal. The goal follows with *for* or *to*: *a strategy for reducing costs*, *a strategy to win back customers*.
entries.pattern: develop a strategy for + noun / -ing / develop a strategy to + verb
examples: The coach **developed a strategy** to slow down their star player, and it worked.
We need to **develop a strategy** for paying off our credit card debt.
The new CEO's first task is to **develop a strategy** for winning back younger customers.

drill.sentence: My sister {{developed a strategy}} for getting her toddler to sleep: same bath, same song, same time every night.
drill.hint: created a careful plan (not *came up with*, *worked out* or *devised*)

entries.related: *come up with a plan* — casual; *devise a strategy* — formal; *map out* — plan something in detail, step by step.

entries.label: noun + noun
entries.meaning: The likelihood that you will keep your job and not be fired or laid off.
entries.usage: Common in conversations about careers, the economy and union contracts. Typical patterns are *offer / provide job security*, *there's no job security* and *for the job security*. It is about keeping a job, not about protection from injury, which is *workplace safety*.
entries.pattern: offer / provide + job security / do something for the job security
examples: She took the government job for the **job security**, even though the pay was lower.
With all the layoffs in tech, nobody in my office feels any **job security** right now.
The new union contract improves **job security** for part-time workers.

drill.sentence: My dad worked at the same factory for forty years; back then, {{job security}} was something people took for granted.
drill.hint: confidence that you won't lose your position (not *stability*)

mistake.why: Many languages use one word for *safety* and *security*; *job safety* means protection from injury at work.

entries.related: *job stability* — similar; *tenure* — permanent job protection, especially for professors and teachers; *precarious work* — the opposite, jobs that can end at any time.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Needing a lot of physical strength, energy or endurance.
entries.usage: Common about jobs, sports and trips, especially in job ads and descriptions: *a physically demanding job*. It sounds neutral and factual, not negative. It goes before a noun or after *be* and *find*, and *mentally* and *emotionally demanding* follow the same pattern.
entries.pattern: a physically demanding + job / role / hike / sport
examples: Nursing is **physically demanding**: you're on your feet for twelve hours.
The hike to the summit is **physically demanding**, so don't try it without some training.
My dad finds moving furniture too **physically demanding** at his age.

drill.sentence: Working on a construction crew in July is {{physically demanding}}, even for young workers.
drill.hint: needs a lot of bodily strength and energy (not *exhausting* or *challenging*)

entries.related: *strenuous* — needing great effort, more formal; *backbreaking* — describes extremely hard physical work; *a desk job* — the opposite, done sitting down.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make new positions of paid work available, through a company, a project or a government policy.
entries.usage: Very common in business news and economic discussion, often with a number: *create 500 jobs*. *Job creation* is the noun form. The opposite is *cut jobs* or *eliminate jobs*.
entries.pattern: create (+ number) jobs / create jobs for + group
examples: The new hospital **created** about 800 **jobs** in its first year.
Opening a second bakery let us **create jobs** for three people from the neighborhood.
Supporters say the stadium will **create jobs**, but critics doubt the numbers.

drill.sentence: Tourism has {{created jobs}} for young people in our town who used to move away after high school.
drill.hint: made new paid positions available (not *brought*, *provided* or *generated*)

mistake.wrong: The new factory will create 300 new workplaces.
mistake.right: The new factory will create 300 new jobs.
mistake.why: A *workplace* is the place where people work (German *Arbeitsplatz* covers both meanings); for positions, English uses *jobs*.

entries.related: *job creation* — the noun; *cut jobs / lay off workers* — the opposite; *generate employment* — more formal.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A job that needs a lot of time, energy, skill or attention, often under high pressure.
entries.usage: Neutral and very common in conversation and career talk; it often explains stress or a lack of free time: *She has a very demanding job*. It can express respect, not only complaint. *Demanding* also describes people: *a demanding boss* expects a lot.
entries.pattern: have / take on + a (very / highly) demanding job
examples: She has **a demanding job** at a law firm, so she rarely gets home before nine.
Being an air traffic controller is **a demanding job** that requires total focus.
Raising twins is **a demanding job**, and no one pays you for it.

drill.sentence: With such {{a demanding job}}, it's no wonder Carlos has no time for hobbies.
drill.hint: work that takes a lot of time and effort (not *stressful* or *tough*)

entries.related: *a high-pressure job* — stress comes from deadlines or high stakes; *a challenging job* — difficult but interesting; *a cushy job* — informal, easy and comfortable.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To help the economy grow faster, for example by increasing spending, jobs or investment.
entries.usage: Very common in news and economic discussion; the subject is often a policy, an event or a type of spending: *Tourism boosts the local economy*. *Boost* sounds livelier and more journalistic than *stimulate*, the technical term. It is often used with *local* or *national*.
entries.pattern: boost the (local / national) economy
examples: City officials hope the music festival will **boost the local economy** this summer.
Cutting interest rates is one way central banks try to **boost the economy**.
Every time my aunt goes shopping, she jokes that she's just **boosting the economy**.

drill.sentence: The government plans to {{boost the economy}} by investing in roads, bridges and rail lines.
drill.hint: make national output increase faster (not *stimulate*, *grow* or *strengthen*)

entries.related: *stimulate the economy* — more technical; *give the economy a shot in the arm* — informal, a quick boost; *slow the economy* — the opposite.

entries.label: quantifier
entries.meaning: A small number of people or things, usually fewer than expected or than you might want.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and news, often to stress that a number is small. It takes a plural noun and a plural verb, and often follows *only* or *just*: *Only a handful of people showed up*. Literally, it is the amount you can hold in one hand (*a handful of nuts*).
entries.pattern: (only / just) a handful of + plural noun
examples: Only **a handful of** students showed up for the 8 a.m. lecture.
Just **a handful of** people in our office know how to fix the copier.
**A handful of** fans waited outside the hotel for hours to get autographs.

drill.sentence: I've only met him {{a handful of}} times, so I don't really know him.
drill.hint: a very small number of (not *a few* or *a couple of*)

entries.related: *a few* — plainer; *a small number of* — more formal; *a handful* (alone) — informal, a difficult child or pet.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To provide enough money to pay for something, either fully or partly.
entries.usage: Common with insurance, budgets and personal money; the subject is often a source of money rather than a person: *My insurance covers the cost of the surgery*. The plural *cover the costs* is also common. *Barely cover the cost of* is a frequent pattern when money is tight.
entries.pattern: X covers the cost of Y / (barely) cover the cost of + noun
examples: My health insurance **covers the cost of** physical therapy, but only for ten sessions.
The money from the bake sale will **cover the cost of** the class trip.
Her part-time job barely **covers the cost of** gas and groceries.

drill.sentence: The airline offered to {{cover the cost of}} our hotel after our flight was canceled.
drill.hint: provide the money for (not *pay for* or *foot the bill for*)

entries.related: *pay for* — plainer; *foot the bill* — informal, pay, often unwillingly; *break even* — earn just enough to cover your costs.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Sleeping deeply, so that you are not easy to wake.
entries.usage: Common in storytelling and conversation, especially about children and pets. *Fast* here means *firmly*, an old meaning of the word. Like *asleep*, it follows a verb (*be*, *fall*, *find someone*) and is not used before a noun.
entries.pattern: be / fall fast asleep
examples: By the time we got home, both kids were **fast asleep** in the back seat.
I called Dan at noon, but he was still **fast asleep** after his night shift.
The dog fell **fast asleep** in front of the fireplace.

drill.sentence: Grandpa sat down to watch the game and was {{fast asleep}} before halftime.
drill.hint: sleeping deeply (not *sound* … or *out cold*)

entries.related: *sound asleep* — the same; *dead to the world* — informal, very deeply asleep; *wide awake* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun + noun
entries.meaning: Time you spend with someone you love, giving them your full attention, without work or other distractions.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation about family and relationships: *spend quality time with* someone. It takes no article: *We need more quality time*, not *a quality time*. It is also used jokingly, for example about time with a pet or the couch.
entries.pattern: spend quality time with + someone
examples: We put our phones away at dinner so we can spend some **quality time** together.
After the divorce, he made sure he got **quality time** with his daughter every weekend.
My idea of **quality time** with my cat is a long nap on the couch.

drill.sentence: Between work and the kids' activities, my husband and I hardly get any {{quality time}} as a couple.
drill.hint: moments of full attention for each other — two words (not *alone …* or *… together*)

entries.related: *family time* — time with family, not necessarily focused; *me time* — informal, time alone for yourself; *bond* — grow closer to someone.

entries.label: adjective + preposition
entries.meaning: To be about a particular topic, or to deal with it as your main interest or task.
entries.usage: Typical of formal and academic writing: *This chapter is concerned with …*, *The study is mainly concerned with …*. Do not confuse it with *be concerned about*, which means *be worried about*. In speech people usually say *be about* or *deal with*.
entries.pattern: X is (mainly / primarily) concerned with Y
examples: The novel **is concerned with** how a family copes with grief after a sudden death.
Our department **is concerned with** patient safety; billing questions go to the front desk.
Most diet books **are concerned with** what you eat, not why you eat.

drill.sentence: Ethics, unlike law, {{is concerned with}} what people should do, not just what they're allowed to do.
drill.hint: has as its main topic — formal (not *is about* or *deals with*)

mistake.wrong: The course is concerned about medieval history.
mistake.right: The course is concerned with medieval history.
mistake.why: *Concerned about* means *worried about*; for the topic of a text, course or job, use *concerned with*.

entries.related: *deal with* — plainer; *focus on* — give special attention to; *be concerned about* — different: be worried about.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To stop operating because the company has failed, usually after losing money.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and news about shops, restaurants and companies. The subject is usually the business, but owners can also say *we went out of business*. *Go bankrupt* is more specific (legally unable to pay debts), and a business can *close down* for other reasons, such as retirement.
entries.pattern: go out of business / be about to go out of business
examples: The bookstore on our street **went out of business** after thirty years.
If sales don't pick up by spring, we'll **go out of business**.
Many small toy stores have **gone out of business** since online shopping took off.

drill.sentence: The video rental store near my house finally {{went out of business}} when everyone switched to streaming.
drill.hint: had to stop operating because it was failing (not *… under* or *closed down*)

entries.related: *go under* — informal, the same; *go bankrupt* — legally unable to pay debts; *stay afloat* — manage to keep going.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A benefit that helps someone succeed and that other people do not have, in a way that seems unjust.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business, school and debates about rules; it is a complaint or an accusation, so it sounds critical. The usual patterns are *give someone an unfair advantage* and *have an unfair advantage over* someone. *Over* introduces the people who lose out.
entries.pattern: give someone / have an unfair advantage (over + someone)
examples: Using a phone during the exam would give you **an unfair advantage** over the other students.
Small shops say the big chains have **an unfair advantage** because they can buy in bulk.
In family volleyball games, my six-foot-five brother's height is **an unfair advantage**.

drill.sentence: The new running shoes were banned because officials said they gave runners {{an unfair advantage}}.
drill.hint: a benefit others didn't have, which wasn't right (not *an edge*)

entries.related: *an edge* — informal, any advantage; *a level playing field* — the opposite, equal conditions for everyone; *stack the deck* — informal, arrange things unfairly.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To officially start examining a crime, an accident or a problem to find out what happened.
entries.usage: Common in news; the subject is usually the police, a government agency, a company or a school. *Launch* sounds more official and dramatic than *start* or *open*. The topic follows with *into*: *launch an investigation into the crash*.
entries.pattern: launch an investigation into + event / problem
examples: Police have **launched an investigation** into a string of car break-ins downtown.
The school **launched an investigation** after several parents complained about the bus driver.
After the food poisoning outbreak, health officials **launched an investigation** to find the source.

drill.sentence: After the bridge collapsed, federal safety officials {{launched an investigation}} into the cause.
drill.hint: officially began to look into what happened (not *opened* or *started*)

entries.related: *open an investigation* — the same, slightly less dramatic; *look into* — informal, examine; *close an investigation* — end it.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A close emotional connection between people, or between people and animals, that is hard to break.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and writing about family, friends, teams and pets. Typical patterns are *have / share / form a strong bond with* someone and *a strong bond between A and B*. *Close*, *deep* and *special* are common alternatives to *strong*.
entries.pattern: form / share a strong bond with someone / a strong bond between A and B
examples: After years on the same soccer team, the girls formed **a strong bond** that lasted into adulthood.
There's **a strong bond** between my grandmother and her dog; they go everywhere together.
Working night shifts together in the ER creates **a strong bond** between nurses.

drill.sentence: Twins often share {{a strong bond}}, even when they grow up in different cities.
drill.hint: a powerful emotional connection (not *close*, *deep* or *special*)

entries.related: *a close bond* — very similar; *a special bond* — unique to two people or animals; *drift apart* — the opposite, gradually become less close.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Completely awake and alert, often at a time when you should or want to be sleeping.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, especially about not being able to sleep: *It's 2 a.m. and I'm wide awake*. It usually follows *be*, *lie*, *stay* or *feel*. *Lie wide awake* is a frequent pattern for nights of worry.
entries.pattern: be / lie / stay wide awake
examples: I had coffee at 9 p.m., and at midnight I was still **wide awake**.
The baby was **wide awake** at 3 a.m. and wanted to play.
She lay **wide awake** all night, worrying about her mother's surgery.

drill.sentence: I was exhausted all day, but as soon as I got into bed, I was {{wide awake}} again.
drill.hint: completely alert, not sleepy at all — two words (not *fully* …)

entries.related: *fully awake* — plainer; *bright-eyed and bushy-tailed* — informal, awake and full of energy; *fast asleep* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To start a planned series of activities, such as ads, events or fundraising, to achieve a particular goal.
entries.usage: Common in news, marketing, charity work and politics. The goal follows with *to* + verb or *for / against* + noun: *launch a campaign to save the library*, *a campaign against drunk driving*. *Launch* suggests an official, public start.
entries.pattern: launch a campaign to + verb / for / against + noun
examples: Parents **launched a campaign** to save the school's music program from budget cuts.
The shoe brand **launched a campaign** on TikTok aimed at teenagers.
Last year, the city **launched a campaign** against littering, with new trash cans and higher fines.

drill.sentence: Local runners {{launched a campaign}} to raise money for a new track at the high school.
drill.hint: began an organized public effort (not *started* or *kicked off*)

entries.related: *kick off a campaign* — informal, the same; *run a campaign* — manage it over time; *call off a campaign* — stop it.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Problems with equipment or technology, such as sound, video or internet, that stop something from working properly.
entries.usage: A fixed, polite phrase used in announcements and at live events: *We're experiencing technical difficulties*. It is usually plural and can sound vague or funny, because it hides what really went wrong. In casual talk people say *tech problems* or *tech issues*.
entries.pattern: experience / have / run into + technical difficulties
examples: The live stream froze for ten minutes because of **technical difficulties**.
We're experiencing **technical difficulties**; please stand by.
Grandma's video call started with the usual **technical difficulties**: we could see her ceiling, but not her face.

drill.sentence: The band's concert started an hour late due to {{technical difficulties}} with the sound system.
drill.hint: problems with the equipment — the polite phrase (not *… problems* or *… issues*)

entries.related: *technical issues / problems* — the same, more casual; *glitch* — a small, short technical problem; *up and running* — working again.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To organize a party and invite people to it, usually at your home or a place you have chosen.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation; *throw* sounds more casual and lively than *have*, *host* or *give* a party. Frequent patterns are *throw someone a party* and *throw a surprise / birthday / going-away party*. The past tense is *threw*.
entries.pattern: throw (someone) a (surprise / birthday) party
examples: We're **throwing a party** on Saturday to celebrate moving into the new place.
Her coworkers **threw her a surprise party** when she retired.
My parents went away for the weekend, so my brother **threw a party**, and the neighbors called the cops.

drill.sentence: For our tenth anniversary, we {{threw a party}} with all the friends who came to our wedding.
drill.hint: organized a celebration — casual verb (not *had* or *hosted*)

mistake.wrong: We're making a party for Anna's birthday.
mistake.right: We're throwing a party for Anna's birthday.
mistake.why: *Make a party* is a direct translation (German *eine Party machen*, Spanish *hacer una fiesta*); English uses *throw*, *have* or *host* a party.

entries.related: *have a party* — the same, neutral; *host a party* — slightly more formal; *crash a party* — go to a party without an invitation.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Private or secret information, such as personal, financial or medical details, that could cause harm if the wrong people saw it.
entries.usage: Common at work, in IT security, law and news about data leaks: *handle / protect / share sensitive information*. In policies it sounds official; in speech it is neutral. *Sensitive data* is a common variant, especially in IT and privacy rules.
entries.pattern: handle / protect / leak + sensitive information
examples: Don't post photos of your boarding pass online; it contains **sensitive information**.
Our HR team handles a lot of **sensitive information**, like salaries and medical records.
The data breach exposed **sensitive information**, including Social Security numbers.

drill.sentence: Your bank will never ask you to share {{sensitive information}} like your PIN by text message.
drill.hint: private details that must be protected (not *personal* or *confidential*)

mistake.wrong: Never send sensible data by email.
mistake.right: Never send sensitive data by email.
mistake.why: *Sensible* means *reasonable* or *practical*; for German *sensibel* in this sense, English uses *sensitive*.

entries.related: *confidential* — officially secret; *classified* — secret for government or military reasons; *public information* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: Strongly criticized, usually by many people or in public.
entries.usage: Common in news and formal writing, usually in the passive: *The plan was heavily criticized by residents*. *Heavily* is a typical intensifier here, like *widely* (by many people) and *sharply* (in strong words). Before a noun it becomes *a heavily criticized decision*.
entries.pattern: be heavily criticized (for + noun / -ing) (by + someone)
examples: The airline was **heavily criticized** for the way it treated passengers during the storm.
The movie's ending was **heavily criticized**, especially by fans of the book.
The referee's decision, **heavily criticized** at the time, turned out to be correct.

drill.sentence: The city's new parking app has been {{heavily criticized}} by drivers who say it charges them twice.
drill.hint: strongly attacked (not *widely*, *harshly* or *sharply*)

mistake.wrong: The new law was hardly criticized.
mistake.right: The new law was heavily criticized.
mistake.why: *Hardly* means *almost not*, so the wrong sentence says the opposite (German *hart kritisiert*); use *heavily*, *harshly* or *sharply*.

entries.related: *widely criticized* — by many people; *harshly criticized* — in severe, unkind words; *highly praised* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To stop doing something that you have done regularly for a long time, usually something bad for you.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and self-help: *break the habit of* + *-ing*, *a hard habit to break*. *Kick a habit* is more informal and is often about addictions like smoking. The opposite is *form a habit* or *get into a habit*.
entries.pattern: break the habit of + -ing / a hard habit to break
examples: I'm trying to **break the habit** of checking my phone the moment I wake up.
Biting your nails is **a hard habit to break**, but bitter nail polish can help.
Her tennis coach helped her **break a bad habit**: dropping her shoulder before every serve.

drill.sentence: My dad smoked for twenty years before he finally managed to {{break the habit}}.
drill.hint: stop for good (not *kick* … or *quit*)

entries.related: *kick the habit* — informal, often about addictions; *get out of the habit of* — gradually stop; *form a habit* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A guess made with almost no information, so it is likely to be wrong.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often to admit you don't really know: *This is just a wild guess, but …* or *If I had to take a wild guess, …*. The usual verbs are *make* and *take*. *Let me take a wild guess* is also used sarcastically when the answer is obvious.
entries.pattern: make / take a wild guess / (just) a wild guess
examples: Nobody knows how many people will come, so any number right now is just **a wild guess**.
I got the trivia question right with **a wild guess**, and my team cheered.
Your shoes are covered in mud. Let me take **a wild guess**: you took the dog to the park?

drill.sentence: I had no idea what the answer was, so I just made {{a wild guess}} and hoped for the best.
drill.hint: an attempt based on almost no information (not *random* or *blind*)

entries.related: *a shot in the dark* — an idiom, the same idea; *an educated guess* — based on some knowledge; *a ballpark figure* — a rough but informed estimate.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To be in a situation where something, often harmful, can affect you, or to have the chance to experience something new.
entries.usage: Common in health, safety and news (*exposed to smoke, radiation, the flu*) and also about experiences (*exposed to music from an early age*). *To* is a preposition, so a verb after it takes *-ing*. Adverbs like *constantly* and *regularly* often go before *exposed*.
entries.pattern: be exposed to + noun / -ing
examples: Firefighters **are exposed to** toxic smoke almost every time they go into a burning building.
Growing up in New York, I **was exposed to** all kinds of food.
If you've **been exposed to** someone with the flu, wash your hands often and watch for symptoms.

drill.sentence: Don't leave the plant in that window; if it {{is exposed to}} direct sunlight all afternoon, the leaves will burn.
drill.hint: has no protection from (not *gets* or *is left in*)

entries.related: *be subjected to* — be forced to experience something bad; *come into contact with* — touch or meet; *be protected from* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To think carefully about the advantages and disadvantages of something before making a decision.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and advice about decisions such as jobs, moves and big purchases. Americans usually say *weigh the pros and cons*; *weigh up* is more British. *Pros and cons* always comes in this order and is also used alone: *What are the pros and cons?*
entries.pattern: weigh the pros and cons (of + noun / -ing)
examples: We spent weeks **weighing the pros and cons** of moving to Denver before we decided to stay.
Before you lease a car, **weigh the pros and cons** carefully.
The doctor helped my mom **weigh the pros and cons** of surgery versus physical therapy.

drill.sentence: I made a list to {{weigh the pros and cons}} of taking the job in Chicago.
drill.hint: think about the good and bad sides (not *compare*)

entries.related: *weigh your options* — compare possible choices; *a cost-benefit analysis* — a formal comparison of costs and gains; *on balance* — after considering everything.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A duty to do something because it is right, not because a law or rule requires it.
entries.usage: Common in serious discussion, ethics, news and personal decisions: *feel a moral obligation to* + verb, *have a moral obligation to* someone. It often contrasts with a legal duty: *not a legal obligation, but a moral one*. The tone is serious, so it can sound heavy in casual talk.
entries.pattern: have / feel a moral obligation to + verb
examples: If you find a lost wallet, you have **a moral obligation** to return it, even if no one would know.
Maya felt **a moral obligation** to care for her stepfather after her mother died.
The company had no legal duty to pay the families, but many people said it had **a moral obligation**.

drill.sentence: Doctors have {{a moral obligation}} to tell patients the truth, even when it's hard to hear.
drill.hint: a duty based on right and wrong, not on law (not *an ethical …*)

entries.related: *a legal obligation* — required by law; *a moral duty* — nearly the same; *a moral dilemma* — a difficult choice between two options.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Completely against a plan, idea or policy and not willing to accept it.
entries.usage: Common in news, meetings and serious conversation, usually after *be*: *Residents are strongly opposed to the new highway*. *To* is a preposition, so a verb after it takes *-ing*. *Firmly opposed* and *bitterly opposed* are close variants.
entries.pattern: be strongly opposed to + noun / -ing
examples: Most parents are **strongly opposed to** moving the school start time to 7 a.m.
My grandmother was **strongly opposed to** tattoos, so I waited until after college to get one.
The nurses' union is **strongly opposed to** the new twelve-hour shift schedule.

drill.sentence: The neighbors are {{strongly opposed to}} the plan to turn the park into a parking lot.
drill.hint: completely unwilling to accept (not *firmly* or *bitterly*)

mistake.wrong: My parents were strongly opposed to buy me a car.
mistake.right: My parents were strongly opposed to buying me a car.
mistake.why: In *opposed to*, *to* is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form, not the base form of a verb.

entries.related: *firmly opposed to* — very similar; *dead set against* — informal, completely against; *in favor of* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To get creative ideas or motivation from a person, place, experience or work.
entries.usage: Common when artists, designers, chefs and writers talk about their influences; it sounds a little formal in casual speech, where *be inspired by* is more natural. Quantity words often come before *inspiration*: *draw a lot of / much / great inspiration from*. The source always follows *from*.
entries.pattern: draw (a lot of) inspiration from + source
examples: The designer **drew inspiration from** her grandmother's old quilts for the new collection.
Many chefs **draw inspiration from** the street food they ate while traveling.
When I'm stuck on a song, I **draw inspiration from** old soul records.

drill.sentence: The architect {{drew inspiration from}} traditional Japanese houses when she designed the new library.
drill.hint: found creative ideas in (not *took* … or *got* …)

entries.related: *take inspiration from* — the same; *be inspired by* — more common in speech; *draw on* — use knowledge or experience.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A close statistical relationship between two things, so that when one changes, the other tends to change too.
entries.usage: Common in research, journalism and talk about data: *a strong correlation between A and B*, *a strong positive / negative correlation*. A correlation does not prove that one thing causes the other, and careful writers say so. In casual talk people say *a strong link* or *connection*.
entries.pattern: a strong (positive / negative) correlation between A and B
examples: There's **a strong correlation** between how much kids sleep and how well they do in school.
Ice cream sales and shark attacks show **a strong correlation**, but only because both go up in summer.
In my house, there's **a strong correlation** between my mood and how much coffee is left.

drill.sentence: Economists see {{a strong correlation}} between a country's education levels and its average income.
drill.hint: a close statistical relationship (not *… link* or *… connection*)

entries.related: *a weak correlation* — the opposite; *causation* — one thing directly causing another; *a strong link* — less technical, common in news.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To finish or stop, especially after continuing for a long time.
entries.usage: Neutral and common in speech and writing about events, periods and relationships: *All good things must come to an end*. It often sounds more emotional or final than plain *end*. *Come to an abrupt end* and *come to a close* are common variants.
entries.pattern: something comes to an (abrupt) end
examples: Sadly, our week in Maine **has come to an end**, and it's back to work tomorrow.
Their twenty-year friendship **came to an end** over a stupid argument about money.
The concert **came to an abrupt end** when the power went out.

drill.sentence: Our long stretch of sunny days finally {{came to an end}} with a huge thunderstorm on Sunday.
drill.hint: stopped after a long time (not *ended* or *drew to a close*)

entries.related: *draw to a close* — slightly more formal, end gradually; *come to a halt* — stop moving; *go on and on* — the opposite, continue for too long.

entries.label: adjective + preposition
entries.meaning: To need something or someone in order to exist, work or succeed.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal; common in writing about money, health, the economy and relationships. The preposition is *on* (*upon* in very formal writing). In speech *depend on* is more common; *dependent* can suggest weakness or a lack of independence.
entries.pattern: be (heavily / financially) dependent on + noun
examples: The town **is heavily dependent on** tourism, so a rainy summer hurts everyone.
At twenty-five, he's still financially **dependent on** his parents.
Our office **is** completely **dependent on** the internet, so a two-hour outage shuts everything down.

drill.sentence: My neighbor stopped driving last year, so now he {{is dependent on}} his daughter for rides to the store.
drill.hint: needs help from — the adjective form (not *relies on* or *reliant on*)

mistake.wrong: The town is dependent from tourism.
mistake.right: The town is dependent on tourism.
mistake.why: German *abhängig von* leads to *from* or *of*; in English, *dependent* and *depend* take *on*.

entries.related: *rely on* — need and trust; *reliant on* — similar, slightly more formal; *independent of* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Something that happens often, so people are not surprised by it.
entries.usage: Neutral to slightly formal; common in news and descriptions of places or routines, often with *become*: *Power outages have become a common occurrence*. It often describes something negative or annoying. In casual talk people say *it happens all the time*.
entries.pattern: be / become a common occurrence (in + place)
examples: Elevator breakdowns are **a common occurrence** in our building.
Flight delays have become **a common occurrence** at this airport since the construction began.
Seeing deer in the backyard is **a common occurrence** where my parents live.

drill.sentence: In this part of Florida, afternoon thunderstorms are {{a common occurrence}} in summer.
drill.hint: something that happens often (not *a daily …*, *a regular …* or *a frequent …*)

entries.related: *a regular occurrence* — happens often and at intervals; *a rare occurrence* — the opposite; *par for the course* — informal, normal and expected (usually bad).

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To stop something, especially something bad, so that it does not continue.
entries.usage: Common in news, speeches and conversation about problems, behavior and conflicts; it sounds decisive. The subject is usually a person, law or event that makes something stop. *Put a stop to* is very close and a little more informal.
entries.pattern: put an end to + noun / -ing
examples: The new landlord **put an end to** the noisy parties in the courtyard.
A knee injury **put an end to** her dream of playing professionally.
Let's **put an end to** this argument and go get some dinner.

drill.sentence: The school installed cameras to {{put an end to}} the vandalism in the parking lot.
drill.hint: make it stop for good (not *put a stop to*)

mistake.wrong: The school wants to make an end to bullying.
mistake.right: The school wants to put an end to bullying.
mistake.why: German *ein Ende machen* leads to *make*; English uses *put an end to* or simply *stop*.

entries.related: *put a stop to* — the same, a little more informal; *bring something to an end* — more formal; *come to an end* — stop by itself.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: Increasing quickly in size, number or importance.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and formal writing, especially before a noun: *a rapidly growing city / company / field / population*. After *be*, both *is growing rapidly* and *is rapidly growing* are fine. *Fast-growing* is the more casual equivalent.
entries.pattern: a rapidly growing + city / company / field / number
examples: Austin is a **rapidly growing** city, and traffic is getting worse every year.
Pickleball is a **rapidly growing** sport, especially among retirees.
A **rapidly growing** number of people now work from home at least one day a week.

drill.sentence: My nephew works for a {{rapidly growing}} startup that has doubled in size every year.
drill.hint: getting bigger very fast (not *fast-…*)

entries.related: *fast-growing* — the same, more casual; *booming* — growing fast and successful; *shrinking* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A sudden and large increase in an amount, number or level.
entries.usage: Very common in news, business and reports about prices, rates and numbers: *a sharp rise in rents*. *In* introduces the thing that increases, while *of* gives the size: *a rise of 20 percent*. The opposite is *a sharp drop* or *a sharp fall in*.
entries.pattern: a sharp rise in + prices / rates / numbers
examples: There's been **a sharp rise in** egg prices since the spring.
Hospitals reported **a sharp rise in** flu cases after the holidays.
After the video went viral, the bakery saw **a sharp rise in** customers.

drill.sentence: The cold snap led to {{a sharp rise in}} heating bills across the state.
drill.hint: a sudden, big upward move in (not *steep*, *spike* or *… increase*)

mistake.wrong: There has been a sharp rise of rents this year.
mistake.right: There has been a sharp rise in rents this year.
mistake.why: Use *in* before the thing that increases and *of* before the amount: *a rise of 10 percent in rents*.

entries.related: *a steep rise* — similar, often over a period of time; *a spike* — very sudden and often short; *a sharp drop* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To start using an idea, plan, method or skill in real situations, not just in theory.
entries.usage: Common in education, work and self-improvement: *put what you've learned into practice*. A short object goes in the middle (*put the plan into practice*), but a long one can come at the end (*put into practice everything we discussed*). *Implement* is the more formal verb.
entries.pattern: put + idea / plan / skill + into practice
examples: I took a cooking class last month, and now I'm **putting** what I learned **into practice**.
It sounds great in theory, but it's hard to **put into practice** when you have three kids.
The hospital **put the new hygiene rules into practice**, and infections dropped within months.

drill.sentence: I learned a few breathing exercises in yoga class and {{put them into practice}} at my next dentist appointment.
drill.hint: used the exercises in a real situation (not *put … to use* or *tried … out*)

entries.related: *put into effect* — make a rule or plan start working, more formal; *implement* — formal; *in theory* — the opposite, as an idea only.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: A level of wealth, comfort and access to goods and services that is good compared with other people or places.
entries.usage: Common in news, economics and conversation about countries, cities and incomes: *enjoy a high standard of living*. *Living standards* (plural) is a frequent alternative in news. *Quality of life* is broader: it includes health, safety and free time, not just money.
entries.pattern: have / enjoy / maintain a high standard of living
examples: Norway has **a high standard of living**, but everything there is expensive.
On two teachers' salaries, it's hard to maintain **a high standard of living** in San Francisco.
My grandparents worked hard so their children could enjoy **a high standard of living**.

drill.sentence: Thanks to its oil money, the country offers its citizens {{a high standard of living}}, with good schools and modern hospitals.
drill.hint: a comfortable, wealthy life (not *quality of life*)

mistake.wrong: Switzerland has a very high life standard.
mistake.right: Switzerland has a very high standard of living.
mistake.why: English does not say *life standard* (from German *Lebensstandard*); use *standard of living* or *living standards*.

entries.related: *quality of life* — includes health and happiness, not just wealth; *the cost of living* — how much basic things cost; *live comfortably* — have enough money.

entries.label: adjective + preposition
entries.meaning: To be closely connected with the subject or situation being discussed, and therefore useful or important to consider.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, essays, job applications and legal contexts: *That's not relevant to the discussion*. *To* is the usual preposition; *relevant for* also occurs, but *relevant to* is much more frequent. The opposite, *irrelevant*, is often used to dismiss a point.
entries.pattern: be (directly / highly) relevant to + topic / someone
examples: Your experience as a lifeguard is actually **relevant to** this job, so put it on your résumé.
The judge ruled that the text messages **weren't relevant to** the case.
I don't see how my age **is relevant to** this conversation.

drill.sentence: My history teacher always tried to show us how the past {{was relevant to}} our own lives.
drill.hint: had real meaning for — adjective + preposition (not *related to* or *connected to*)

entries.related: *pertinent to* — formal, the same; *related to* — connected, but not necessarily useful; *beside the point* — not relevant.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To treat something as especially important and give it a lot of attention.
entries.usage: Formal; common in reports, descriptions of schools and companies, and speeches: *The program places great emphasis on teamwork*. Words like *great*, *strong* and *too much* often come before *emphasis*. *Put emphasis on* is more neutral, and *focus on* is more common in speech.
entries.pattern: place (great / strong / too much) emphasis on + noun / -ing
examples: The new coach **places great emphasis on** defense, so practice is mostly drills.
Our pediatrician **places a lot of emphasis on** sleep, not just diet and exercise.
Too much **emphasis is placed on** grades and not enough on curiosity.

drill.sentence: The hotel {{places great emphasis on}} customer service; the staff greet every guest by name.
drill.hint: treats as especially important (not *puts* … or *… importance on*)

mistake.wrong: Our school lays great value on good manners.
mistake.right: Our school places great emphasis on good manners.
mistake.why: *Lay value on* translates German *Wert legen auf*; English says *place* or *put emphasis on*, or simply *values* good manners.

entries.related: *put emphasis on* — the same, slightly less formal; *stress* — say clearly that something is important; *play down* — the opposite, make something seem less important.

entries.label: compound adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A romantic relationship between two people who live far apart, often in different cities or countries.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation; typical patterns are *be in a long-distance relationship* and *make a long-distance relationship work*. *Long-distance* takes a hyphen before a noun. Informally, people also say *we're doing long distance*.
entries.pattern: be in / make work + a long-distance relationship
examples: We were in **a long-distance relationship** for two years: she was in Boston and I was in Seattle.
My parents don't believe **a long-distance relationship** can work, but we're proving them wrong.
Cheap flights and video calls make **a long-distance relationship** much easier than it used to be.

drill.sentence: When he got into a college across the country, they decided to try {{a long-distance relationship}} instead of breaking up.
drill.hint: staying a couple while living far apart

entries.related: *doing long distance* — informal, being in one; *a whirlwind romance* — short and intense; *break up* — end a relationship.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To make someone feel relaxed and comfortable, especially when they are nervous.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and in descriptions of doctors, teachers, hosts and interviewers: *She has a way of putting people at ease*. The person goes between *put* and *at ease*. *Make someone feel at ease* is a common alternative.
entries.pattern: put someone at ease (right away / with + something)
examples: The dentist told a few jokes to **put** my son **at ease** before the checkup.
As an interviewer, Rachel has a gift for **putting** people **at ease**.
The pilot's calm voice **put** me **at ease** when the plane hit turbulence.

drill.sentence: The nurse chatted about the weather to {{put me at ease}} before the blood test.
drill.hint: help me relax (not *calm me down*)

entries.related: *make someone feel at home* — welcome a guest warmly; *calm someone down* — when they are upset; *make someone uneasy* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Really interested in something or someone, not just pretending in order to be polite.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, dating and job interviews: *He seemed genuinely interested in what I had to say*. *Genuinely* makes clear that the interest is real, which matters when people might suspect politeness. *Genuinely* also goes with *surprised*, *sorry* and *helpful*.
entries.pattern: be / seem genuinely interested in + noun / -ing
examples: My new manager seems **genuinely interested in** my ideas, which is refreshing.
Kids can tell when you're **genuinely interested in** what they're saying.
He asked so many questions about my hometown that I could tell he was **genuinely interested**.

drill.sentence: She wasn't just being polite; she was {{genuinely interested in}} hearing about my trip to Peru.
drill.hint: honestly curious about (not *really*, *truly* or *sincerely*)

mistake.wrong: She seemed genuinely interested about my work.
mistake.right: She seemed genuinely interested in my work.

entries.related: *sincerely* — honest in feelings, more formal; *politely interested* — showing interest only to be nice; *feign interest* — pretend to be interested.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A person or thing that is obviously better than all the others, or that won easily.
entries.usage: Common in sports, elections, reviews and everyday comparisons: *There was no clear winner*, *emerge as a clear winner*. It is also used informally for personal choices: *For me, the pasta was the clear winner*. *No clear winner* means the result was close.
entries.pattern: be / emerge as a clear winner / there's no clear winner
examples: Emma's homemade astronaut suit was **a clear winner** in the costume contest; nobody else came close.
The school debate ended without **a clear winner**, so the judges called it a tie.
In our test of six vacuum cleaners, the cheapest one was **a clear winner**.

drill.sentence: We asked the kids which beach they liked best, and there was {{a clear winner}}: the one with the ice cream stand.
drill.hint: one that was obviously the best (not *… favorite*)

entries.related: *the hands-down winner* — informal, the same; *a close call* — hard to decide; *a tie* — no winner.

entries.term: tell the difference between two things
entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To see, hear, taste or understand how two similar things are different.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, especially with *can't*, *couldn't* and *Can you …?*: *I can't tell the difference between the two*. It can stand alone (*I can't tell the difference*). *Tell A from B* and *tell them apart* are close alternatives.
entries.pattern: (can't) tell the difference between A and B
examples: Can you **tell the difference between** the cheap olive oil and the expensive one?
My grandma can't **tell the difference between** a text and an email.
Kids need to learn to **tell the difference** between news and ads online.

drill.sentence: In a blind test, most people can't {{tell the difference}} between tap water and bottled water.
drill.hint: recognize how they differ (not *taste* … or *see* …)

mistake.wrong: I can't make the difference between the two wines.
mistake.right: I can't tell the difference between the two wines.
mistake.why: *Make a difference* means *have an effect*; to recognize how things differ, use *tell* (French *faire la différence* leads learners to *make*).

entries.related: *tell A from B* — the same, shorter; *tell them apart* — distinguish two similar people or things; *distinguish between* — more formal.

entries.label: adjective + preposition
entries.meaning: To be the most important thing for achieving or understanding something.
entries.usage: Common in business, sports, health and advice: *Communication is key to a good marriage*. *Key* here has no article, but *the key to* means the same. *Key* can also stand alone at the end of a sentence: *Timing is key*.
entries.pattern: X is key to + noun / -ing
examples: Getting enough sleep **is key to** staying healthy during flu season.
Their goalie **was key to** the team's win last night.
Good communication **is key to** making any relationship work.

drill.sentence: Patience {{is key to}} learning the guitar; nobody sounds good at first.
drill.hint: is the most important thing for — no article (not *crucial*, *vital* or *essential*)

entries.related: *the key to* — the same with an article; *crucial to* — very important for; *make or break* — decide success or failure.
